analysis.investment_thesis: Birla Corp trades at a borderline attractive earnings yield (~11.2% EBIT/EV) but earns a poor ~11.6% ROIC — well below Greenblatt's 20%+ threshold — disqualifying it as a Magic Formula buy. Cement's capital intensity structurally prevents this from being a "good business at a cheap price."
key_strengths: Earnings yield of ~11.2% (EBIT INR 1,221 Cr / EV ~INR 10,893 Cr) is approaching the 12% attractive zone
FCF sharply improving: INR 1,226 Cr in FY2025 vs INR 179 Cr in FY2023; borrowings declining from INR 4,462 Cr to INR 3,489 Cr
Revenue CAGR of 12.2% over 9 years with 62.9% promoter holding signals operational stability
key_risks: ROIC of ~11.6% (EBIT/Invested Capital: 1,221/10,518 Cr) is far below Greenblatt's 20% hurdle — cement's massive fixed asset base destroys returns
Net profit is volatile and contracting — INR 630 Cr (FY2021) → INR 40 Cr (FY2023) → INR 295 Cr (FY2025); ROE at 4.79% is deeply unimpressive
Finance costs of INR 327 Cr consume 27% of EBIT, leaving thin buffer; EBITDA trend is contracting
red_flags: ROCE of 7.08% is below the cost of debt — the business is earning less than it pays lenders
EBITDA contracted from INR 1,723 Cr (FY2021) to INR 1,284 Cr (FY2025) despite 36% revenue growth — margin compression is severe
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula: Earnings Yield = EBIT (INR 1,221 Cr) / EV (Market Cap INR 7,521 Cr + Debt INR 3,489 Cr – Cash INR 118 Cr = INR 10,892 Cr) = 11.2% — just shy of the 12% attractive threshold. ROIC = EBIT / Invested Capital (Equity INR 7,147 Cr + Debt INR 3,489 Cr – Cash INR 118 Cr = INR 10,518 Cr) = 11.6% — barely half of Greenblatt's 20% minimum. Neither metric qualifies Birla Corp for the Magic Formula screen. The EV/EBITDA of 6.74x looks optically cheap, but cheap businesses with poor returns are value traps, not Magic Formula opportunities.

The fundamental problem is structural: cement is one of the most capital-intensive industries imaginable. Birla Corp has grown revenue 12.2% annually for 9 years yet net profit CAGR is only 6.5%, and EBITDA is now contracting. The large CWIP spike (INR 2,551 Cr in FY2022) has translated into assets but not proportionate earnings — a classic capital destruction pattern. The one genuine positive is the FCF turnaround (INR 1,226 Cr in FY2025) and rapid debt paydown, suggesting the heavy capex cycle is behind them. This warrants a HOLD rather than an outright avoid, but it is not a business Greenblatt would rank highly.
